query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings operating at high temperature, sliding induces dynamic grain refinement and partial amorphization in the near‐surface region. This ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer—formed or enhanced by a controlled post-deposition annealing treatment—leads to an inverse Hall–Petch behavior that impedes dislocation motion, lowers the friction coefficient, and reduces wear by distributing the contact stress more uniformly.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu HEA thin coating on a conventional metal substrate exhibiting a relatively coarser, mixed microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition annealing treatment (e.g., 500°C for a set period) to promote dynamic grain refinement and partial amorphization compared to the baseline as-deposited condition.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (around 500°C) in an inert or controlled atmosphere (to minimize oxidation) under representative load and sliding speed, where the inverse Hall–Petch effects are expected to be active.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline and partially amorphous near-surface layer that acts as a barrier to dislocation motion and shear localization.
generation.mechanism: During sliding at elevated temperatures, the energy input and heat facilitate a dynamic structural transformation in the HEA coating. The refined grains lead to an inverse Hall–Petch effect that increases the local shear strength, reducing the ease of dislocation propagation. This mechanism retards wear and favors a smoother microscopic deformation profile by effectively distributing stress over a highly refined surface layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline (un-annealed coating), the annealed coating should exhibit a lower friction coefficient, reduced wear rate, and display microscopic deformation characterized by fewer and less pronounced strain bursts (i.e. less serrated behavior), as evidenced by the formation of a refined, near-amorphous surface film.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating without additional annealing treatment, under the same high-temperature sliding test conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is predicted to hold in high-temperature sliding regimes (∼500°C) under inert or controlled atmospheres. In environments where oxidation is significant or if thermal gradients disrupt the formation of the ultrafine layer, the mechanism may not be active.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in friction and wear resistance is not precisely known, as the kinetics of grain refinement and the extent of amorphization may vary with annealing parameters; further fine-tuning may be required to optimize the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu HEA-coated samples: one set receives the controlled annealing treatment (e.g., 500°C for a defined duration) to induce the refined near-surface structure, while the second set remains in the as-deposited state. Perform sliding wear tests at 500°C in an inert atmosphere for both sets. Conduct microstructural analysis (via TEM/SEM) to verify the formation of the ultra-nanocrystalline or partially amorphous surface layer, and record friction coefficients and wear rates.
measurements: Microstructural imaging (grain size, phase state) from TEM/SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant decrease in friction and wear rate relative to the as-deposited samples, or if microstructural analysis does not confirm the formation of a markedly refined (ultra-nanocrystalline or partially amorphous) surface layer, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
